stories.headline: Update: Major TV Networks Decline to Air Trump's Primetime Election Security Address
stories.summary:
ABC News and NBC News announced Thursday they will not broadcast President Trump's evening Oval Office address on their main cable networks, instead streaming it on digital platforms. Trump is expected to deliver remarks on election integrity and declassified findings related to interference in the 2020 election, though White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said the speech could also address the Iran conflict and economic matters.

The decisions by the networks have intensified an already bitter feud between major broadcasters and the Trump administration. FCC Chairman Brendan Carr has ordered reviews of licenses held by ABC-owned local stations following disputes over coverage, including ads run during The View and remarks by late-night host Jimmy Kimmel about first lady Melania Trump.

The move drew criticism from both ends of the political spectrum. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) urged networks to refuse to platform what she called 'lies,' while several Republicans, including outgoing Sen. John Cornyn (R-TX), called on the president to focus on the 2026 midterms rather than relitigating 2020. Leavitt urged all networks to carry the speech live, saying Americans deserve to hear from the president directly.

ABC said it would provide anchored coverage on ABC News Live and radio, and air a post-speech special report on the broadcast network. NBC said its streaming service NBC News NOW would carry the address live, followed by a network special report. The speech is scheduled for 9 p.m.

stories.headline: Update: Taco Bell Removes Lettuce From Some Locations as FDA Probes Supplier in Cyclospora Outbreak
stories.summary:
Taco Bell announced Thursday it is pulling lettuce from a portion of its restaurant locations after the FDA opened an investigation into iceberg lettuce supplied by Taylor Farms as a possible source of the nationwide cyclospora outbreak. Reports linking Taylor Farms specifically to the outbreak first emerged Thursday evening, marking a concrete new development in an ongoing public health crisis.

The outbreak has now spread to 34 states, according to multiple reports. Federal and Michigan state officials had already begun investigating Taco Bell earlier in the week, but the identification of Taylor Farms as the suspected supplier represents the most specific lead yet in the effort to trace the contamination's origin.

Cyclospora is a microscopic parasite that causes intestinal illness, typically transmitted through contaminated food or water. The current outbreak, which has grown to nearly 4,000 cases, has been among the largest cyclospora events in recent U.S. history, and health authorities had previously struggled to pinpoint a common source across the affected states.

stories.headline: Algeria Foster Care Home Fire Kills 11, Including Children
stories.summary:
A fire at a foster care facility in the Mohammadia suburb of Algiers killed at least 11 people and injured 19 others in the early hours of Thursday morning, Algerian authorities confirmed. The blaze began around 3:30 a.m. local time and required 10 fire engines and 16 ambulances to respond. Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune confirmed in a social media post that children were among the dead, calling the incident a 'tragic loss.'

The cause of the fire has not been determined. The tragedy comes amid a severe heatwave in Algeria that has produced nearly 1,000 fires across the country in the span of a week, with authorities recording 115 wildfires in the 24 hours preceding the foster home blaze alone. Five people with special needs were evacuated and transported to safety during the incident.

Prime Minister Sifi Ghrieb visited hospitals in Algiers to see the injured. Opposition parties and social media users have demanded a transparent investigation and legal accountability for any safety failures or negligence at the facility.

stories.headline: Australia Summons Laos Ambassador Over 'Deeply Frustrating' Charges in Backpacker Methanol Deaths
stories.summary:
The Australian government summoned Laos' ambassador to Canberra on Thursday after reports emerged that Laos intends to pursue charges carrying a maximum penalty of only one year in prison and a fine of roughly A$1,600 against those responsible for the deaths of six foreign tourists — including two Australians — who died after drinking methanol-laced alcohol at a hostel in Vang Vieng in November 2024. Foreign Minister Penny Wong called the development 'deeply frustrated and bitterly disappointed.'

Bianca Jones, 19, and Holly Morton-Bowles, 19, were among the six victims. British, American, and Danish tourists also died after consuming free drinks tainted with methanol — a toxic substance sometimes illegally mixed into alcohol to cut costs — at the Nana Backpacker Hostel. Earlier this year, ten people connected to the hostel received only suspended sentences and fines of $185 each on evidence-destruction charges, a result widely condemned by victims' families.

The father of one victim said feeling 'furious would be an understatement,' while another father called it 'very hard to comprehend' that six lives would be valued at less than a year of imprisonment. Australia appointed a special envoy, Pablo Kang, to travel to Laos on Friday to formally convey the government's objections and explore further avenues for accountability. Laos has not yet officially confirmed the charges but was expected to hold a press conference.

stories.headline: Trump Imposes 25% Tariffs on Brazilian Goods, Sparking Retaliation Threat
stories.summary:
The Trump administration announced a 25% tariff on a broad range of Brazilian imports, escalating a trade dispute the White House says stems from Brazil's treatment of U.S. technology companies, ethanol producers, and other American industries. The tariffs include exemptions for key consumer staples such as coffee, beef, and rare-earth materials, which the administration says is intended to limit inflationary effects on American consumers.

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's office called the move "a regrettable milestone" in bilateral relations and accused the White House of acting under pressure from allies of former far-right President Jair Bolsonaro, whose family has maintained ties to Trump-aligned circles. Brazil has vowed reciprocal tariffs against U.S. goods in response.

The announcement comes just months before Brazil's October presidential election, injecting trade tensions into an already deeply polarized domestic political environment. Analysts say the tariffs could disadvantage Lula heading into the vote while potentially boosting opposition candidates aligned with Bolsonaro.

The move is the latest in a series of aggressive U.S. trade actions under Trump's second term. Supporters argue the tariffs are a necessary correction to unfair Brazilian trade practices, while critics warn they risk damaging relations with one of the Western Hemisphere's largest economies and could raise costs for U.S. industries that rely on Brazilian inputs.

stories.headline: Update: Texas Floods Strike Same Region as Last Year's Deadly Disaster, at Least One Dead
stories.summary:
At least one person has died and roughly 80 rescues have been carried out as catastrophic flooding again strikes central Texas, with the Guadalupe River — the same waterway that killed more than 130 people last July — rising 32 feet in just four hours on Thursday. Texas Governor Greg Abbott declared the flooding a life-threatening emergency and urged residents in Uvalde, Kerr, and Kendall counties to evacuate immediately, warning that rivers would continue to surge throughout the day.

The National Weather Service in San Antonio issued urgent warnings describing "catastrophic" flooding in progress, and videos from the region showed vehicles submerged to their windows, families being carried to safety by rescuers wading through brown floodwaters, and wildlife struggling to stay afloat. Last year's floods, which originated from the same river system, killed 25 children and two counselors at Camp Mystic, an all-girls summer camp near Kerrville that subsequently filed for bankruptcy and did not reopen this year.

Residents described the current flooding as worse than last year in some affected communities. Boerne resident Carter Lopez, 30, said he helped pull neighbors from rising water near his apartment building after floodwaters inundated ground-floor units overnight.

This marks the second consecutive day of severe flooding in South Texas, compounding concerns about emergency preparedness and infrastructure vulnerability in a region that has now suffered back-to-back catastrophic flood seasons along the same river system.

stories.headline: Update: Canadian Wildfires Spread Hazardous Smoke Across U.S. Midwest and Northeast
stories.summary:
More than 850 wildfires burning across Canada — including 30 new fires that ignited Thursday — are sending hazardous smoke plumes deep into the United States, with air quality alerts now spanning the Upper Midwest, Great Lakes region, and parts of the Northeast. Detroit ranked as the city with the worst air quality in the world on Thursday, according to Swiss tracker IQAir, followed by Minneapolis, Chicago, and Toronto.

The U.S. National Weather Service said parts of Michigan and Minnesota recorded "hazardous" air quality readings, prompting health advisories for sensitive groups to remain indoors. New York activated its air quality emergency protocols and opened hundreds of cooling centers across the city, distributing KN95 masks as conditions in the metro area reached "unhealthy" levels. Concerns are also mounting that smoke could affect air quality in New Jersey, where Sunday's FIFA World Cup final is scheduled to take place at MetLife Stadium.

In Ontario, a fire in the northern part of the province forced evacuations from First Nations communities, with one chief describing her settlement as having been "burnt to ashes." Canadian authorities say northwesterly winds will continue pushing smoke south through the weekend before a shift in wind direction is expected to improve conditions in the U.S. early next week.

Republican state lawmakers in Michigan sent an open letter to Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney demanding better wildfire management, saying their "patience has run out" after three consecutive years of cross-border smoke impacts. U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra offered a more measured response, commending firefighting cooperation between the two countries.

stories.headline: Rubio Convenes 60-Nation Conference on "Left-Wing" Political Terrorism Ahead of Midterms
stories.summary:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Thursday hosted delegations from more than 60 countries at a State Department conference focused on what the Trump administration characterizes as a rising global threat from left-wing political terrorism. Rubio described the issue as a longstanding "blind spot" in international counterterrorism doctrine and called on allied governments — mostly from Europe and Latin America — to unite against what he termed "communists and Marxists" engaging in political violence.

The conference is part of a broader Republican political strategy ahead of November's midterm elections, with President Trump and his allies repeatedly framing the Democratic Party's progressive wing as an existential threat to American institutions. Trump has accused Democratic opponents of supporting political violence, and the administration has elevated left-wing extremism as a marquee campaign issue.

Data from the Center for Strategic and International Studies presents a more complicated picture. While left-wing terrorism incidents in the U.S. did surpass right-wing incidents for the first time in over 30 years as of mid-2025, the researchers note the shift reflects both a sharp drop in far-right incidents and a modest rise from a very low baseline on the left — averaging five left-wing incidents annually versus one on the right in the most recent period tracked, compared with historical averages of roughly 23 right-wing incidents per year from 2016 to 2024. The report's authors caution that right-wing violence could easily return to elevated levels.

Critics, including Democratic lawmakers, have accused the administration of misrepresenting terrorism data to score political points, while supporters argue the conference represents a legitimate effort to address an undercovered dimension of extremist violence. The event underscores how terrorism and political violence have become central flashpoints in the lead-up to the 2026 midterm elections.

stories.headline: Update: ICE to Equip All Field Offices with Body Cameras Within 60 Days
stories.summary:
The Department of Homeland Security announced Wednesday that half of all U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement field offices now have body cameras for agents, with the remaining offices expected to receive them within 60 days. The announcement marks a significant acceleration of a years-long effort to outfit ICE agents with cameras and comes amid intense scrutiny of the agency's use-of-force practices.

Pressure for expanded camera use has mounted sharply in recent days following fatal shootings of two immigrant fathers by federal immigration agents. In neither incident were the officers involved wearing body cameras, the agency confirmed. The shootings have fueled calls from civil liberties advocates, Democratic lawmakers, and some Republicans for greater accountability and transparency in immigration enforcement operations.

The Trump administration has defended its enforcement posture as necessary to carrying out the president's immigration agenda, while critics argue the lack of cameras in earlier incidents reflects a systemic accountability gap. The new 60-day timeline represents a concrete policy response to those concerns, though advocates say implementation and footage-access policies will determine whether the cameras produce meaningful oversight.

The body camera rollout follows a series of high-profile use-of-force incidents that have drawn congressional attention and public protests. How footage will be reviewed, retained, and made available to the public or legal proceedings remains an open question as the agency moves toward full deployment.

stories.headline: Trump Announces Veterans Will Automatically Qualify for CDLs to Replace Deported Immigrant Truckers
stories.summary:
President Trump announced Wednesday at the Pennsylvania Defense and Innovation Summit that military veterans who have driven heavy trucks in service will be automatically eligible for a commercial driver's license, positioning them as replacements for undocumented truck drivers the administration is moving to deport. Trump said his administration would soon take "historic action" to remove illegal immigrant truck drivers from American roads, citing safety concerns including drivers who "can't read signs" or are impaired.

Trump's remarks were delivered in the context of the death of Pennsylvania State Trooper Michael Pahira Jr., killed this month in a crash involving Haitian national Michael Bon, who held a CDL renewed in early 2025 while his humanitarian parole was still technically active. The Trump administration says Bon's parole was terminated in June 2025; Bon's defense attorney says his client held a valid work permit at the time of the license renewal and suffered from an untreated medical condition that may have caused the crash.

The broader policy push builds on a February directive by Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy requiring all commercial truck driving license tests to be conducted in English only, following an audit finding some states were issuing CDLs to holders of expired work permits. Industry analysts warn that a rapid removal of immigrant truck drivers could exacerbate existing driver shortages in an already strained freight sector.

Supporters of the president's approach argue that immigration enforcement must extend to industries with public safety implications, and that veterans represent an underutilized workforce pipeline. Critics, including transportation industry groups and immigration advocates, contend that mass deportation of CDL holders would disrupt supply chains and that the policy conflates immigration status with road safety in ways not supported by broader accident data.

stories.headline: Update: Trump Directs ICE to Resume Traffic Stops Despite Two Recent Fatal Shootings
stories.summary:
President Trump publicly stated Wednesday that Immigration and Customs Enforcement should continue conducting vehicle traffic stops, pushing back against a suspension of the practice that followed two fatal shootings of individuals who were not the original targets of ICE operations — one in Houston, Texas, and one in Biddeford, Maine. Trump's statement puts him at odds with the temporary suspension order, and DHS Acting Deputy Secretary Brian Mullin posted on X that he and the president want ICE officers to "have all options available," without directly confirming whether traffic stops would resume.

The Houston shooting on July 7 killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, whose family and attorneys dispute DHS's account that he attempted to ram officers with his vehicle. The Maine shooting killed Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero; ICE said he attempted to flee a traffic stop. Texas Governor Greg Abbott, a Trump ally, called for a Texas Rangers investigation while saying immigration enforcement can be achieved "without shooting people." Democrats and local officials in both states have demanded independent investigations.

The DHS green card rule is a separate but related immigration development filed Thursday: USCIS announced a new rule, set to take effect in 60 days, that will again weigh applicants' use of Medicaid, food stamps, and housing assistance when determining green card eligibility — restoring Trump's first-term "public charge" standard that the Biden administration narrowed. USCIS Director Joseph Edlow said the rule reaffirms "the requirement of self-reliance" and is expected to affect hundreds of thousands of applicants.

Supporters of the administration frame both moves — resuming traffic stops and tightening the public charge rule — as necessary enforcement of existing immigration law and protection of public resources. Critics, including Democratic lawmakers and immigration advocacy groups, argue the traffic stop deaths demonstrate dangerous overreach and that the welfare rule will deny legal status to working families who use benefits to which they are legally entitled.

stories.headline: Argentina Face FIFA Discipline After World Cup Semi-Final Falklands Banner Against England
stories.summary:
Argentina players celebrated their dramatic 2-1 comeback victory over England in the World Cup semi-final in Atlanta on Wednesday by holding a banner reading "Las Malvinas son Argentinas" — "The Falklands are Argentine" — on the field, prompting an immediate diplomatic response and the prospect of FIFA disciplinary proceedings. The defending champions will face Spain in Sunday's final.

The British government swiftly condemned the gesture. Prime Minister's official spokesperson said: "The World Cup might not be ours, but the Falkland Islands definitely are. Our commitment to the Falklands will never waver." Liberal Democrat leader Ed Davey wrote to FIFA president Gianni Infantino calling for the players involved to be suspended from the final, drawing a parallel to UEFA's one-game suspension of Spain players Álvaro Morata and Rodri after they chanted "Gibraltar is Spanish" during Euro 2024 celebrations.

FIFA previously fined the Argentine Football Association £20,000 in 2014 when players held an identical banner before a friendly against Slovenia, citing rules on political action and team misconduct. There is also precedent for player bans: South Korea's Park Jong-woo received a two-match suspension after the 2012 Olympics for holding a territorial-claim banner. FIFA typically processes disciplinary action in the weeks following a tournament, making it unlikely the players would be barred from Sunday's final.

The Falkland Islands, a British overseas territory roughly 300 miles off Argentina's coast, have been the subject of a sovereignty dispute since Argentina's 1982 invasion, which resulted in a 74-day war and the deaths of 655 Argentine and 255 British servicemen. The banner's appearance in a match between the two countries during a World Cup on U.S. soil gives the incident heightened political and sporting significance.

stories.headline: Update: Uganda Discharges Last Ebola Patient as Congo Outbreak Surpasses 2,000 Cases
stories.summary:
Uganda has discharged its last confirmed Ebola patient, leaving the country with no active cases and beginning a mandatory 42-day countdown before it can officially be declared Ebola-free. Health Minister Dr. Chris Baryomunsi called the development "a moment of joy," noting Uganda recorded only 20 confirmed cases and two deaths — mostly among visitors from the neighboring Democratic Republic of Congo, where the outbreak originated.

The situation in DRC remains severe and worsening. Government data show more than 2,000 confirmed infections and 796 deaths, though a World Health Organization official warned this week that the true infection count could be four times higher, as the virus may have circulated undetected for months before the outbreak was formally declared. The U.S. has tightened travel restrictions, now requiring American citizens who have been in DRC to spend 21 days in a third country before returning home, replacing an airport-screening protocol.

The new U.S. entry rule has raised concerns among global health workers. Franklin Graham, CEO of an organization running Ebola treatment centers in DRC, told Reuters the policy could hamper recruitment of American medical personnel and reduce the scale of international response operations in affected areas.

Uganda's rapid containment — built on decades of outbreak experience, isolation protocols, contact tracing and targeted public health messaging — is being held up as a model. Authorities have nonetheless urged citizens to remain vigilant and seek immediate care for symptoms including fever, vomiting, diarrhea, or unexplained bleeding.

stories.headline: Volunteer Firefighter Investigated as Suspect in Fontainebleau Forest Fire That Burned 2,000 Hectares
stories.summary:
French authorities have placed an 18-year-old volunteer firefighter under formal investigation on suspicion of starting the Fontainebleau forest fire south of Paris, which has burned more than 2,000 hectares (roughly 5,000 acres) and forced approximately 1,000 people to evacuate. Prosecutor Diane Ngomsik told AFP the suspect initially confessed to "setting fire to twigs with a lighter and petrol" before retracting the statement. A second 18-year-old man has also been placed under formal investigation. The fire has been contained but not fully extinguished.

Visiting the site on Thursday, President Emmanuel Macron pledged zero leniency for arsonists and stated France had not seen so many wildfires since World War Two. Fontainebleau forest is home to the Palace and Park of Fontainebleau, a UNESCO World Heritage Site; Macron said 10 percent of the forest has been burned. No fatalities have been reported. The blaze partially closed France's main north-south motorway for several days.

The fire is one of nearly 11,000 recorded in France since the start of 2026. Across Europe, record-breaking summer temperatures have driven major wildfire events, most lethally in Spain where at least 13 people have been killed. A large wildfire has also spread across more than two miles of the Cairngorms National Park in Scotland. Algeria is simultaneously battling roughly 1,000 fires within a single week, linked to an ongoing heatwave.

Scientists attribute the escalating fire conditions to climate change: Europe is warming at twice the global average rate, according to the Copernicus climate service, producing more intense and frequent summer heatwaves and drier vegetation across the continent.

stories.headline: Update: Todd Blanche Faces Senate Confirmation Hearing, Confronts Epstein Files Questions
stories.summary:
Attorney general nominee Todd Blanche appeared before the Senate Judiciary Committee Wednesday, facing pointed questions from Democrats about the Justice Department's handling of Jeffrey Epstein-related records. Sen. Dick Durbin (D-IL) demanded Blanche personally meet with 10 Epstein victims within 30 days. Blanche said he was legally prohibited from directly contacting victims represented by counsel but that DOJ officials were prepared to meet with their attorneys immediately and could arrange such a meeting "as soon as today." He noted the department had already reviewed more than 6 million pages of documents under the Epstein Files Transparency Act.

The hearing produced a sharp partisan exchange over which party bore more responsibility for delays in releasing Epstein records. Sen. Marsha Blackburn (R-TN) argued Democrats had blocked Epstein-related subpoenas when they controlled the Senate; Durbin disputed that account, saying he had repeatedly tried to recognize Blackburn for amendments on Epstein flight logs but was blocked by Republican procedural maneuvers. Blanche acknowledged some victim information was improperly disclosed in earlier document releases but said steps had been taken to correct the error.

Separately, former Obama White House counsel Kathryn Ruemmler appeared in a closed-door House Oversight Committee session the same day, facing bipartisan criticism over her years-long relationship with Epstein after her resignation from Goldman Sachs. Emails released by the DOJ showed she met with Epstein numerous times and exchanged gifts with him between 2014 and 2019, years after his 2008 conviction. Ruemmler denied any wrongdoing and said she was unaware of criminal conduct.

The dual Capitol Hill proceedings made Wednesday one of the most active days yet in Congress's overlapping Epstein investigations. The Blanche confirmation hearing carries particular weight given his role would give him authority over ongoing federal probes. The hearing drew coverage from 25 outlets across the political spectrum.

stories.headline: IOC Lifts Russia Olympic Ban Despite Ongoing Ukraine War, Sparking International Backlash
stories.summary:
International Olympic Committee president Kristy Coventry announced last week that Russia will be permitted to return to international Olympic competition, ending a ban that began following a massive state-sponsored doping scandal in 2014 and was extended after Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine. The decision has drawn sharp condemnation from athletes, governments, and human rights advocates who argue Russia has made no concessions to justify the reinstatement. More than 16,000 Ukrainian civilians have been killed since the invasion began, with casualty rates increasing in 2026.

Coventry defended the move by saying the IOC does not want to "hold athletes accountable for the actions of their governments," a position critics called contradictory given that the IOC had already created a neutral-flag pathway for vetted individual Russian athletes during the ban. Opponents note that Russia has not withdrawn from Ukraine, curtailed its military operations, or accepted accountability for the doping program that prompted the original ban.

The decision has drawn criticism from across the political spectrum. Even President Donald Trump, who has sought to broker a peace deal with Russia, has expressed frustration with Vladimir Putin's refusal to negotiate. U.S. Olympic Committee and allied national bodies are facing pressure to formally object to the reinstatement before the next Games.

The reinstatement is seen by critics as the latest instance of the IOC prioritizing commercial interests over political principles, echoing earlier controversies over the 2008 and 2022 Beijing Games. The story was covered by 12 outlets.

stories.headline: Jones Act Waiver Extension Weighed as Iran Conflict Disrupts Global Oil Supply Chains
stories.summary:
The White House is considering a third extension of its Jones Act waiver as the ongoing U.S.-Iran conflict continues to disrupt oil and gas supply chains through the Strait of Hormuz. Administration officials met this week to discuss whether to extend the waiver, which currently expires August 16 and allows foreign-flagged ships to transport fuel between U.S. ports. A White House official said no decision has been made but emphasized the waiver has helped prevent domestic supply shortages.

The move faces resistance from within the Republican Party. More than 50 GOP members sent a letter to President Trump urging the waiver to expire, arguing the Jones Act is critical to the American maritime and shipping industry. The law normally requires goods transported between U.S. ports to be carried on U.S.-built, U.S.-flagged, and U.S.-crewed vessels.

The Iranian Revolutionary Guard has threatened to keep the Strait of Hormuz closed until U.S. strikes cease and has also threatened to close the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a key gateway to the Red Sea. Despite the escalating threats, oil prices remained relatively stable Wednesday, with Brent crude at approximately $84.66 per barrel and West Texas Intermediate near $79.25. U.S. Central Command confirmed another wave of strikes against Iranian military targets was launched Wednesday.

The Jones Act debate illustrates the domestic economic strain produced by the prolonged conflict. Energy analysts warn that prices could rise if the Hormuz closure extends further into summer, and the waiver debate has placed the administration at odds with a significant bloc of its own congressional supporters. The story was covered by 9 outlets.

stories.headline: Poland Charges Ukrainian Teen with 47 Counts of Russian-Directed Sabotage
stories.summary:
Polish prosecutors have charged an 18-year-old Ukrainian national, identified as Illia K., with 47 criminal acts carried out between November 2024 and August 2025 on behalf of Russian intelligence. Authorities say the suspect desecrated memorials to Polish victims of the World War II Volyhnia massacre, vandalized the Monument to the Jewish Heroes of the Warsaw Ghetto, and made preparations to fly a drone over Polish President Karol Nawrocki's motorcade during last year's Armed Forces Day parade. He was arrested three days before that event.

Poland's Internal Security Agency said the operations were designed to "incite ethnic tensions between Poland and Ukraine" by exploiting painful historical grievances over the wartime UPA massacres, which claimed up to 100,000 Polish lives. The suspect allegedly acted primarily for financial gain, receiving cryptocurrency payments traced to accounts registered in Russia and China. He faces a potential life sentence if convicted.

The case is part of a broader pattern flagged by Polish security services: the ABW launched 48 espionage investigations in 2025, more than double the prior year, and says Russia has systematically sought to exploit Polish-Ukrainian historical tensions to weaken Western unity. The charges come at a diplomatically sensitive moment, as the issue of the Volyhnia massacre has already strained bilateral ties — Polish President Nawrocki recently stripped Ukrainian President Zelensky of Poland's highest state honor over a military unit naming dispute.

The arrest highlights Russia's continued use of hybrid warfare tactics, including recruiting foreign nationals for sabotage operations inside NATO member states. Poland is a key transit country for Western military aid to Ukraine, making destabilization efforts there of particular strategic concern.

stories.headline: Protests Erupt in Ukraine After Zelensky Fires Popular Defence Minister Fedorov
stories.summary:
Crowds gathered in Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities Thursday after President Volodymyr Zelensky abruptly dismissed Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, a 35-year-old tech-focused reformer appointed only in January. Demonstrators held signs reading "Hands off Fedorov" and "Stop sabotaging victory!" as Zelensky offered no public explanation for the decision. Ukrainian lawmakers were scheduled to vote Thursday on confirming Interior Minister Ihor Klymenko as Fedorov's replacement.

Fedorov had been credited with modernising Ukraine's war effort, driving anti-corruption reforms, expanding drone warfare programmes, and using data analytics to improve battlefield performance. His dismissal drew sharp criticism from soldiers and civil society. "This is the worst mistake Zelensky has made during his entire presidency," one Ukrainian soldier told the BBC. Some analysts linked the firing to tensions between Fedorov and Commander-in-Chief Oleksandr Syrskyi; others cited perceived delays in overhauling military mobilisation.

The ouster is significant because Fedorov had become a symbol of Ukraine's high-tech asymmetric warfare strategy at a critical juncture in the conflict with Russia. His ministry played a key role in recent drone strikes on Russian-occupied Crimea, and he had pressed Elon Musk to block Russian use of Starlink — a move that disrupted frontline Russian operations. His removal raises questions about the direction of Ukraine's defence policy as the war continues.

In a Facebook post following his dismissal, Fedorov listed his ministry's achievements and vowed to "continue to defeat the enemy through asymmetry, speed of innovation." The episode reflects mounting internal tensions within Ukraine's wartime leadership at a moment when Western support and battlefield momentum remain in flux.

stories.headline: TSMC Pledges Additional $100 Billion for U.S. Chip Production, Raising Total Commitment to $265 Billion
stories.summary:
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company announced Thursday it will invest an additional $100 billion in Arizona, bringing its total U.S. commitment to $265 billion and potentially adding four new fabrication plants to the eight already planned or under construction in the state. The announcement, welcomed by the Commerce Department as a major job-creation milestone, came alongside TSMC's disclosure of a 77 percent jump in second-quarter net profit to $22 billion, driven by soaring demand for advanced chips powering artificial intelligence data centres.

TSMC chief executive CC Wei said the timeline for the new plants would depend on market conditions. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick credited President Trump's trade and tariff pressure with spurring the investment, noting a deal struck in January that cut U.S. tariffs on Taiwanese goods to 15 percent in exchange for large-scale investment commitments. TSMC produces the most advanced chips used by companies including Nvidia and Apple, making its U.S. expansion a central element of the administration's semiconductor supply-chain strategy.

The announcement underscores the broader U.S. push to reduce dependence on Asian chip manufacturing exposed during Covid-era supply shortages. TSMC is now Asia's most valuable company, with a market capitalisation of approximately $2 trillion and a share price up more than 55 percent this year. The scale of the investment represents one of the largest foreign corporate commitments to American manufacturing in recent history.

The expansion is expected to generate tens of thousands of American jobs, according to the Commerce Department, though specific employment figures and construction timelines were not provided. Wei acknowledged the investment will reinforce the U.S. semiconductor ecosystem and strengthen supply chains critical to both consumer technology and national security.

stories.headline: Update: Genoa Bridge Collapse Trial Reaches Verdict After Nearly Eight Years
stories.summary:
A Genoa court delivered a first-instance verdict Thursday in the trial over the August 2018 collapse of the Morandi bridge, which killed 43 people and triggered one of Italy's worst infrastructure disasters in decades. Fifty-seven defendants — including former executives of toll road operator Autostrade per l'Italia, engineers from maintenance firm Spea, and former transport ministry officials — faced charges ranging from multiple manslaughter to falsifying documents. All defendants had denied wrongdoing throughout the nearly four-year trial spanning 284 hearings.

Prosecutors argued that maintenance was repeatedly delayed and warning signs ignored while profits continued to flow, while defence lawyers contended the real cause was a design flaw in the specific cable that failed and that no maintenance programme could have prevented the collapse since the cable was encased in concrete. Some lesser charges, including document forgery, had already lapsed under Italy's statute of limitations before Thursday's ruling.

Family members of the 43 victims gathered in the courtroom to hear the verdict, describing years of anguish and anxiety awaiting accountability. "After so many years, so many hearings, we may be able to see some light," said Egle Possetti, whose sister, brother-in-law and two nephews were among those killed. Former deputy chief prosecutor Francesco Pinto cautioned that appeals and a final Supreme Court ruling could extend proceedings by another two and a half years.

The case has fuelled a broader national debate in Italy about the condition of ageing public infrastructure and accountability within the private concession system that managed the country's motorways. One defendant, former Atlantia chief executive Giovanni Castellucci, was already serving a separate six-year sentence for a fatal viaduct collapse in southern Italy in 2013.

stories.headline: Pakistan Refuses to Accept Deportation of Rochdale Grooming Gang Leader Released from UK Prison
stories.summary:
Pakistan's government has publicly rejected British pressure to accept the deportation of Shabir Ahmed, a ringleader of the Rochdale grooming gang who was released from prison this month after serving a 22-year sentence for multiple counts of rape and sexual offences against girls as young as 13. Pakistani Foreign Ministry spokesman Tahir Andrabi told the BBC that Ahmed — stripped of his British citizenship following his 2012 conviction — is "entirely an internal matter of the United Kingdom" and that Pakistan "has no connection whatsoever with this matter."

Ahmed arrived in Britain in the late 1960s and was one of nine men convicted of exploiting girls at two Rochdale takeaway restaurants. Under the Immigration Act 1971, Commonwealth citizens who arrived before 1973 and had lived in the UK for five years cannot be deported, a legal barrier that has blocked Ahmed's removal. The UK government has proposed amending the law so that serious foreign criminals would no longer benefit from those protections, but any deportation still requires Pakistan to formally accept him.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood acknowledged this week that Ahmed's removal depends on Pakistani cooperation, saying the 1971 Act "should not be used as a bar against removal in cases like that of Shabir Ahmed." Following his release, Ahmed was placed in 24-hour staffed accommodation and fitted with a GPS monitoring tag, with authorities warning he would be returned to prison if he breached strict licence conditions. Victims said they were "frightened" and felt "unsafe" following his release.

Pakistan's response creates a significant diplomatic obstacle for the British government, which has faced intense public and political pressure to remove Ahmed from the country. The standoff highlights the legal and diplomatic complexities surrounding the deportation of dual nationals convicted of serious crimes, and comes amid heightened national debate in the UK over grooming gang prosecutions and immigration enforcement.
